title: Ecotherapy: Using nature to treat health

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Ecotherapy is a new profession, still unrestrained by such things as professional practices and licensing requirements. It can mean regular outdoor sessions with a therapist or simple exercises by yourself, and is usually a supplement when treating a medical condition. It is not intended as a replacement for standard, evidence-based treatments. J Phoenix Smith is an ecotherapist, a practitioner of nature-based exercises intended to address both mental and physical health. This means he can recommend a variety of unusual therapies: listening to birdsong five minutes every day; starting a garden, and tracking the seeds’ growth; or sitting in a park for half an hour once a week without checking your phone.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Ecotherapy training programs are springing up around the United States, but the one that got Smith started in the field was launched by a pioneer of the movement, Craig Chalquist, the chair of the East-West Psychology Department at the California Institute of Integral Studies. His knowledge of this subject is wideranging, but one popular example is: ‘If you hold moist soil for 20 minutes, the soil bacteria begin elevating your mood. You have all the antidepressant you need in the ground.’ As it turns out, Chalquist was referring to a study published in Neuroscience, a prestigious journal, that had found that soil bacteria called Mycobacterium vaccae increase serotonin, a chemical that improves our mood, in the brains of mice. Antidepressant medications work in the same way.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Some of the simple principles behind ecotherapy are gaining acceptance even in mainstream medicine. When a licensed doctor recommends treatment based on these principles, it tends to carry more weight. For example, at his office in Washington, D.C., Dr. Robert Zarr, a pediatrician, advises his obese, diabetic, anxious or depressed patients about which park they should visit, on which days, and for how long and other relevant information – just as though he were giving medical prescriptions. He says giving such information is more important than repeating some vague statement such as ‘exercise more’. Zarr is part of a small but growing group of health-care professionals who are essentially medicalizing nature. He relies on a list of 382 local parks – the product of meticulous mapping and rating, based on accessibility, safety, and amenities – that he helped create for a community-health initiative in Washington, D.C.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A prescription to go to a park is a low-risk, low-cost intervention that, in Zarr’s experience, people are quick to accept. People are more likely to move around in a park than while watching TV, but there may be more to it than that. Researchers in the United Kingdom found that when people did workouts in natural settings instead of a gym, or other artificial environments, they experienced less anger, fatigue, and sadness. They also found that patients released from hospitals after a period of surgery healed faster and with fewer complications when their home looked out on trees rather than just a wall.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Why would living in natural environments be more therapeutic for us than in man-made ones? ‘That gap [in our understanding], we don’t fully understand,’ says Richard Louv, a well-known journalist whose recent book, Last Child in the Woods, is widely credited with starting the modern American nature-exposure movement. He points to research that says people are attracted to and feel restored by looking at images of open landscapes, particularly savannas. Also restorative, according to an influential essay by Roger S Ulrich on health-care facility design, are slow-moving water, bushes, and birds or other unthreatening wildlife. He explains the effect in evolutionary terms: natural environments trigger upbeat emotions because watching the environment was once important for human survival. According to E O Wilson, a famous biologist, we’re genetically programmed to ‘affiliate with other forms of life,’ and when we don’t, we suffer and can develop ‘nature-deficit disorder.’

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The answer may also have to do with nature’s capacity to instill a sense of awe. At a conference at UC Berkeley, scientists gathered to discuss the latest research on the health benefits of this sensation, including reductions in levels of cortisol, a stress hormone. However, what makes ecotherapy different from an attempt to mine nature for its beneficial effects,’ Chalquist explained – ‘is that we have to give something back.’ He tells students that if they want to experience the full value of ecotherapy, they can’t just go touch a tree in a forest; they need to come to care about that tree and help preserve it for future generations. In fact this tends to be one of the more persuasive arguments for ecotherapy. If its practice leads people to volunteer at a local park or to join a nature club or to fall in love with a specific redwood tree, it could legitimately improve their health by providing them with a sense of purpose. And even if people practicing ecotherapy don’t give back to nature, it’s tough to argue against a doctor who tells you to spend more time in a park.
